Both research types must guard against model and code errors, measurement or observation data bias, irreproducible processing, and extrapolation of conclusions. items.title: What do employers usually look at in hiring?

values: Materials and setup｜all fictional data
The following contains two teaching materials, a physics pendulum and an astronomical light curve. Neither is measured data; use only paper or script calculations and do not build an apparatus.

A1 physics: take g = 9.8 meters per second squared and the small-angle model T = 2 pi times the square root of L over g; L = 0.25, 0.36, and 0.49 meters, with fictional T = 1.01, 1.20, and 1.42 seconds, and a reading uncertainty of plus or minus 0.03 seconds each.

A2 astronomy: the normalized brightness on days 0, 1, 2, and 3 is 1.00, 0.96, 1.00, and 1.03; the reading uncertainty for each point is plus or minus 0.02, and the instrument, time scale calibration, and repeat observations are not given.
Tasks and deliverables
Compute the three theoretical periods and residuals in A1, noting the formula, meters, and seconds; plot T squared against L.

Compute the day 1 brightness difference relative to day 0 and the given reading uncertainty in A2, plot the four-point light curve, and list the celestial events that cannot be confirmed from four points.
Reference approach (complete it yourself first)
The theoretical periods in A1 are about 1.00, 1.20, and 1.40 seconds; the third residual is about +0.02 seconds and cannot prove new physics.

In A2 the day 1 brightness is 0.04 lower than day 0. If the two plus or minus 0.02 values are mutually independent standard uncertainties, the difference has a standard uncertainty of about the square root of (0.02 squared +0.02 squared) = 0.028; but the problem gives no calibration, systematic error, or repeat observations, so four points cannot confirm a transit or a period.
Boundaries and review
Keep the original fictional values, formulas, charts, units, and revision records; do not operate a real pendulum apparatus or telescope, and do not publicly announce a celestial discovery.

entries.answer: Physicists study physical laws and verify them with theory, experiment, or simulation; astronomers study celestial bodies, plan observations, analyze telescope data, and publish results. The two task sets are in O*NET 19-2012 and 19-2011 respectively, and BLS 19-2010 is only a combined statistic.
entries.question: What do physicists and astronomers do every day?

entries.answer: BLS uses 19-2010 to aggregate the wages, employment, and openings of physicists and astronomers. It does not mean the two occupations have exactly the same tasks or individual wages.

title.text: Physicist and astronomer career guide: tasks, wages, and entry paths

subject.name: Physicists and astronomers
subject.summary: Physicists and astronomers (United States BLS 19-2010 combined statistics) study the laws of matter, energy, and celestial bodies. Physicists may focus on theory, experiment, or application; astronomers may use ground-based and space instruments to observe celestial bodies, analyze data, and propose models. Both must state assumptions, errors, and reproducibility. The BLS combined wages and employment cannot be used as the figures for either standalone occupation, and O*NET tasks and interests must be verified separately for 19-2011 and 19-2012.
